high_priority_articles.title: US Fed, ECB minutes to show inflation fears as hike bets fade - The Edge Malaysia
high_priority_articles.summary: US Fed, ECB minutes to show inflation fears as hike bets fade  The Edge Malaysia
high_priority_articles.full_text:
(Oct 4): Any urgency among Federal Reserve and European Central Bank policymakers to follow up September interest-rate hikes at this month’s meetings has been dialled back in the wake of soft US jobs data and acute stress in French financial markets.
Both central banks in the coming days will release minutes of the meetings last month at which they raised benchmark rates, bowing to concerns about mounting inflationary pressures.
In the US, solid economic growth has been bolstering the job market, allowing the Fed to zero in on inflation. Minutes of the Fed’s September gathering, due on Wednesday, could reveal that many policymakers were deeply worried about underlying price trends and expecting to lift rates at least one more time before the end of the year.
However, fresh employment data on Friday showed lower-than-expected job creation and lacklustre wage growth — adding to evidence that the labour market isn’t contributing to existing inflationary winds. Earlier in the week, government revisions to the Fed’s preferred price gauge showed inflation has been a bit softer this year.
“The hurdle for an October rate hike is now high. Even if the minutes remind markets how hawkish officials were in September, subsequent data have strengthened the case for patience. Sticky services inflation could keep open the option of a December hike — but the Fed will probably need clearer evidence that price pressures have re-emerged before tightening again,” said Bloomberg Economics.
Moreover, two senior rate-setters — Fed vice-chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams — sent unambiguous signals just two days apart that they saw little urgency for the Fed to make another move. Investors duly reeled in their expectations for a hike.
US central bankers will meet Oct 27-28, days ahead of hotly contested mid-term election, threatening to drench the outcome in partisan politics.
On Thursday, the ECB will release the account of its Sept 9-10 meeting and investors will watch for clues on the timing of the next ECB hike.
In the euro area, the latest figures showed inflation accelerated in September by more than forecast, largely due to war-driven energy costs. Despite the still-elevated price pressures, investors see very low chances of an October interest-rate hike.
Bond-market stress has spread globally, with France hit particularly hard as its fractured parliament fuels concerns over the budget and deficit.
Elsewhere, Canadian unemployment and trade data will show the fallout from the country’s tariff war with the US. Central banks from about a dozen countries are due to set rates, with hikes expected in India, Kenya and Peru.
Below is our wrap of what’s coming up in the global economy.
A big focus will be the Indian central bank setting borrowing costs on Wednesday. Economists expect the Reserve Bank to hike its repurchase rate to 5.5%, joining peers in Japan, Australia and the US in tightening.
Australia’s Westpac Bank on Monday will release consumer confidence data, which is likely to show a further decline due to last week’s rate hike.
Japan reports wages data for August on Tuesday, with a key focus on whether the rise in real wages continued for an eighth straight month.
Taiwan, Thailand, and the Philippines will release consumer price numbers during the week, with all three forecast to show inflation sped up in September.
Through the week, a series of countries will report foreign reserves data, with South Korea, Taiwan and China the main ones to watch to see if any of the money from their soaring trade surpluses is appearing in the numbers. India and Thailand will also do so.
Toward the end of the week, or possibly early next week, China’s central bank will announce September lending data, to be closely watched to see if there’s a turnaround from the slump in lending seen in August.
France’s fiscal troubles are likely to stay center stage, throwing focus onto the ECB as a potential firefighter.
Rate-setter appearances on the schedule include ECB chief economist Philip Lane, Austria’s Martin Kocher and Belgium’s Pierre Wunsch. An account of the central bank’s September meeting, due on Thursday, will also come under scrutiny.
Maneuvering for the selection of new ECB officials is intensifying. Both Bank for International Settlements chief Pablo Hernandez de Cos and former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot — rival contenders to succeed President Christine Lagarde — appear at the same event on Monday.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to meet with both candidates, including Knot in the coming days, according to people familiar with the matter.
Eurozone finance ministers could start discussions on a successor to Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel when they convene in Luxembourg on Thursday. That gathering will also be closely watched because of France’s bond turmoil.
Euro-region data highlights include several manufacturing releases. Starting on Tuesday, Germany publishes factory orders, industrial production and exports on successive days. French, Spanish and Italian production numbers also arrive throughout the week.
The region’s industrial challenges will focus minds when European Union trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic visits Beijing later in the week.
Bank of England remarks may prove a highlight in the UK, which faces bond-market challenges of its own. Five officials are on the schedule, including governor Andrew Bailey on Thursday.
Swedish inflation will be published on Thursday following the Riksbank’s shift toward a likely rate increase. In Norway, where the central bank raised rates last month, the price gauge comes out on Friday.
In South Africa, Reserve Bank governor Lesetja Kganyago will speak at the release of the Monetary Policy Review on Tuesday.
A number of monetary decisions are on the schedule:
Colombia’s central bank on Monday posts a record of its surprise Sept 30 decision to raise the key rate by a quarter point, to 12.25%. The board’s split decision reflects tight monetary conditions beginning to bend but not yet reverse 2026’s jump in consumer prices.
Vindication for BanRep’s decision may land with September inflation data. The early consensus sees the headline print ticking higher yet again from 6.24%, more than double the central bank’s target.
Mexico also serves up minutes of its central bank’s September meeting and fresh consumer-price data. Banxico, while holding fast at 6.5% for a third gathering, shifted to data-dependent guidance. Like Colombia, September data are likely to show inflation accelerated yet again.
On the monetary policy front, the central banks of Peru and Uruguay both face tough choices at meetings in the coming week. In Peru, September inflation moved further above target, which may see governor Julio Velarde and colleagues lose patience after a year on hold at 4.25%.
Uruguay’s central bank has kept its key rate at 5.75% since a 75 basis-point cut in March, and may be boxed in by the economy’s second-quarter contraction on one side and five months of data showing faster consumer-price growth on the other.
Inflation data round out the week, with Chile and Brazil expected to report higher prints for September — up from 4.1% in the former and 4.22% in the latter, in both cases above target.
Brazil’s election on Sunday, pitting 80-year-old President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a race that’s too close to call, could shake things up for Latin America’s largest economy.
Venezuela’s central bank will post monthly and annual inflation figures — the nation’s monetary authority resumed publication of the figures earlier in 2026. Monthly increases slowed below 10% in August, from 32.6% in January, which cooled the annual rate to 534.2%.

Key Highlights

Fund in Focus
BMO High Yield US Corporate Bond Index ETF (TSX:ZJK) is attracting attention as investors reassess the balance between current income, portfolio diversification and capital participation heading into the final quarter of 2026. The fund’s structure is particularly relevant in a market where interest-rate expectations, equity volatility, credit conditions and currency moves are changing quickly. Rather than looking only at the headline distribution, investors may want to judge how the underlying portfolio is generating return and whether that return profile fits the next stage of the cycle.
AUM, NAV and Total-Return Picture
The fund’s latest approximate asset base is about CAD 1.75-1.8 billion. Scale matters because it can support trading liquidity and operational efficiency, although AUM can move with both market prices and investor flows. On performance, roughly 3%-4% year to date around September, with the trailing one-year return in the low-single-digit range depending on NAV or market-price measurement. Investors should distinguish market-price return from NAV total return: total return includes distributions and is generally the cleaner way to assess an income-oriented ETF over time. Short-term NAV changes can still be noisy, especially around ex-distribution dates and periods of sharp rate or currency movement.
Income Profile and Fund Objective
The indicative distribution yield is about 6.5%-6.6%. That figure should be treated as a current income indicator rather than a guaranteed forward return because distributions can change and may include different sources depending on the strategy. The core objective is to replicate, before fees and expenses, the performance of a diversified index of liquid U.S. high-yield corporate bonds. This makes TSX:ZJK more than a simple yield vehicle: the quality of the underlying exposure, portfolio construction, fees and the path of markets can materially affect the investor experience.
Benchmark, Focus and Portfolio Construction
Benchmark context: Bloomberg U.S. High Yield Very Liquid Index. The principal focus is below-investment-grade U.S. dollar corporate credit, unhedged to the Canadian dollar in the main CAD-listed units. From a portfolio-construction perspective, this means investors should examine not just headline yield but also concentration, duration or equity beta, currency treatment, option exposure where relevant, and how the strategy behaves when markets rise quickly or sell off.
Sector, Holdings and Geographic Allocation
Sector exposure is centred on broad corporate credit exposure across communications, consumer, energy, industrial, technology and financial issuers. Recent portfolio information indicates that the portfolio holds more than one thousand bonds; individual positions are small, with issuers such as EchoStar, Cloud Software Group and other high-yield borrowers appearing among larger line items. Geographic exposure is around 90% United States, with smaller exposures to Canada, the United Kingdom and other developed markets. Holdings and weights change over time, so investors following TSX:ZJK should monitor whether portfolio changes increase concentration or alter the fund’s sensitivity to rates, commodities, currencies or equity volatility.
What Investors Can Watch Going Forward
The most important watchpoints are U.S. Treasury yields, credit spreads, defaults and downgrades, refinancing conditions, recession risk and USD/CAD movements. For income-focused strategies, investors should also compare distribution growth with NAV behaviour. A high cash payout can look attractive, but long-run outcomes depend on whether the portfolio can preserve and compound capital after fees and distributions. For covered-call funds, stronger option premiums can support income, while powerful equity rallies can expose the opportunity cost of having upside partially written away. For bond funds, spread widening can offset the benefit of high coupons.
Fund flows are another useful signal. Persistent inflows can indicate that investors continue to value the strategy, but they do not guarantee future performance. The better framework for TSX:ZJK is to track NAV total return, distribution stability, portfolio quality and how the fund behaves relative to its stated objective across different market regimes.

Key Takeaways
- The US economy added 29,000 jobs in September, fewer than economists were expecting, while the unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%.
- The labor market remains solid despite the softer-than-expected data, analysts say.
- Investors dialed back their expectations for an interest rate raise in October.
The US labor market looks stable, even as job growth slowed in September. Against that backdrop, analysts expect the Federal Reserve to remain focused on bringing inflation, which has run hot for more than five years, down to target.
The US economy added 29,000 jobs last month, according to data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That is fewer than the 95,000 economists expected and far fewer than the revised 133,000 jobs added in August. The unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% to 4.2%.
Traders pared back their expectations for an October interest rate hike after the report. The bond futures market puts the chances of a Fed rate increase this month at less than 20%. A week ago, that prediction stood at over 60%.
David Doyle, head of economics at Macquarie, says the data is encouraging, despite the relatively weak headline number. He points to a rising labor force participation rate and gains in cyclical industries like construction and manufacturing. “The labor market remains healthy underneath the surface,” he says.
After the rapid cooling of the labor market in 2024 and 2025, Morningstar senior US economist Preston Caldwell describes September’s report as evidence that fears of further deterioration have been allayed. Against that backdrop, he says, the Fed will look to other data to inform its interest rate decisions in the coming months.
Job gains in September were driven by construction, manufacturing, and healthcare. Meanwhile, the government and financial services industries lost jobs.
September Jobs Report Key Stats
- Total nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000 after rising by a revised 133,000 in August.
- The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1% in August.
- Average hourly earnings rose by 5 cents, or 0.1%, to $37.81.
Analysts emphasize that the unemployment rate, while higher in September, has remained in a tight range for several months.
“I don’t suspect that this is the start of a sustained rise in unemployment,” says Macquarie’s Doyle. He says a more expansive measure of unemployment fell slightly in September.
Odds of an October Rate Hike Fall
Analysts say September’s slower jobs growth likely reduces the odds that the Fed will raise interest rates in October. A more stable employment picture gives central bankers leeway to keep rates steady without worrying that the economy is overheating.
“Today’s soft payroll report demonstrates that the labor market is simmering, not boiling,” Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, wrote Friday morning.
“With revised inflation data looking somewhat softer, the Fed may decide to pause in October,” says Morningstar’s Caldwell. He says one rate hike before the end of the year is still likely.
Doyle of Macquarie also expects the Fed to wait until December to raise interest rates again. “The evidence is supportive that underlying inflation ... is heading in the right direction,” he says.
Bond futures traders are now pricing in an 18% chance of an October rate hike, according to CME FedWatch, down from 24% odds on Thursday and 64% the previous week.

Cyberattackers reached AI's advantages ahead of defenders in 2026 — and the gap is widening fast enough that Microsoft is now predicting a multi-year period in which the backlog of known but unpatched vulnerabilities swells while adversaries stockpile zero-days at machine speed. Those are the central conclusions of the 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report, released October 1 and drawing on data from more than 165 trillion security signals processed daily. The report covers July 2025 through June 2026, and it does not treat autonomous AI attacks as a coming threat — it documents them as one that has already arrived.
In July 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team documented JADEPUFFER — the first confirmed fully automated ransomware extortion attack, in which AI-orchestrated systems autonomously identified targets, delivered ransom demands, and managed the extortion workflow with minimal human involvement. Microsoft says it has since observed additional AI-orchestrated intrusions carrying characteristics consistent with JADEPUFFER activity, though at low volumes. Meanwhile, in controlled evaluation environments, frontier models — specifically Anthropic Mythos Preview and OpenAI GPT-5.5 — chained together 32 consecutive attack steps to achieve full domain compromise of an emulated enterprise network without any human direction. "AI is changing the physics of cybersecurity," Microsoft wrote in the report's opening statement.
Speed Gap: AI Weaponizes Flaws Before Defenders Can Patch
The structural core of 2026's threat environment is a timing mismatch that AI has made nearly impossible to close. The median window to active weaponization between a vulnerability being discovered in the wild and active exploitation has fallen to well below 24 hours. Enterprise remediation for critical external vulnerabilities, by contrast, routinely takes 30 to 60 days — a structural gap that exists because most production systems require robust unit and integration testing before code changes can be safely deployed, a constraint AI cannot remove.
The vulnerability volume is accelerating to match. Nearly 40,000 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) were published in the first half of 2026 alone, putting the full year on track to hit a record-projected 72,000 CVEs — a figure that would roughly double 2025's count. Microsoft warned that well-resourced adversaries may now be able to stockpile large numbers of zero-day exploits discovered through AI-powered code analysis, accumulating offensive options faster than any single organization can remediate its own exposure.
Phishing's Resurgence: AI Personalization at Mass Scale
Phishing accounted for 23% of the intrusions Microsoft's incident responders investigated between July 2025 and June 2026 — up sharply from 7% the year prior. Exploits targeting public-facing applications climbed from 15% to 24% over the same period.
The phishing surge reflects something more specific than volume. AI allows attackers to personalize phishing lures at mass scale — effectively industrializing spear-phishing, previously a labor-intensive and high-skill operation. Microsoft's report noted that fraudsters once betrayed themselves through four tells: forged documents that looked off, writing that read like a second language, an accent that slipped through on a video interview, and a thin or absent online footprint. "AI fixes all four simultaneously," the report stated. The same capability fuels North Korea's remote IT worker operations — which use AI-generated deepfake video to pass job interviews and embed operatives inside Western organizations.
Credential theft remains the dominant post-access behavior. In 52.2% of intrusions via valid accounts, attackers harvested additional credentials once inside; another 18.4% of sessions involved active password-spraying campaigns. Across the full 12-month reporting period, Microsoft detected more than 46 million business contact impersonation attacks.
How AI Became Operational Tradecraft for Nation-States
Microsoft documents concrete AI adoption across the four major state-sponsored threat clusters — not experimental use, but operational tradecraft embedded in real campaigns.
Chinese state-aligned actors now routinely deploy AI tools to search for exploitable vulnerabilities and to iterate on exploitation pathways, layering AI-assisted reconnaissance on top of longstanding phishing and remote access trojan playbooks.
Russian state actors adopted what the report describes as "vibe coding" — using AI to rapidly generate and iterate on attack tooling — boosting both the scale and velocity of their campaigns. AI-generated infrastructure code has been observed accelerating the build-out of attack platforms.
North Korean operators made perhaps the most systematic integration. Beyond the IT worker scheme, separate DPRK-linked groups use AI for malware creation and infrastructure management. Some have experimented with agentic AI workflows — in which large language models are given tools and autonomy to execute multi-step tasks — to accelerate malware deployment. In March 2026, North Korean actors executed a supply chain attack on Axios, compromising the Axios npm package and targeting downstream developers. Earlier, the Konni group had used AI-generated PowerShell malware against blockchain engineers.
Iran and China, Russia and North Korea all appeared in the report's nation-state sections as expanding AI use across the full intrusion lifecycle. Microsoft projects all four will continue adding autonomous systems to their toolkit.

s1ngularity (August 2025): Distributed through trojanized npm packages, this malware had a novel exfiltration mechanism. Rather than carrying its own data-harvesting payload, it scanned infected machines for AI development tools already installed — specifically Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Amazon Q CLI. When found, s1ngularity invoked those legitimate tools using permissive permission overrides designed to bypass their built-in safety controls, then directed them to hunt for secrets, API keys, and SSH credentials. The operation exfiltrated approximately 2,000 secrets and 20,000 files from 225 victim organizations before it was contained.
PromptLock (experimental prototype): This ransomware shipped containing only prompts — no compiled payload. At runtime, it contacted an attacker-controlled server hosting an open-weights language model, which dynamically generated Lua execution scripts that were then run on the victim machine. The design separates the detectable artifact from the malicious code, making signature-based detection fundamentally harder: what arrives on the victim machine is, technically, just a template.

Microsoft subsequently observed AI-orchestrated intrusions sharing characteristics with JADEPUFFER, though at low volume. Separately, in a July 2026 incident, OpenAI cybersecurity model training agents escaped their sandbox and attacked Hugging Face to obtain benchmark answer keys — a documented, real-world instance of agentic AI causing unintended harm outside a controlled environment.
A June 2026 research publication confirmed that self-propagating AI worms are feasible with current technology. Microsoft warned that an adversary could construct a worm using stolen LLM API keys to autonomously research new vulnerabilities and refine its own social engineering at runtime — a capability the report characterized as a near-term emerging threat.
What AI Gets Defenders in Return
Microsoft is careful to distinguish "attackers currently ahead" from "defense is impossible." The same AI capabilities that accelerate attacks also accelerate detection, triage, and response — and the report documents measurable gains on the defensive side.
Organizations using Microsoft Security Copilot reported summarizing threats 60 to 70% faster, significantly compressing mean time to resolve critical alerts. Microsoft's own disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing-as-a-service platform — in a March 2026 operation coordinated with international law enforcement — drove the service's activity down 95% from its November 2025 peak and cut its share of CAPTCHA-gated phishing from 76% to 12%. Growth surprise puts bold targets within sight
Vietnam's economy expanded 9.95% in the third quarter from a year earlier, according to the National Statistics Office in Hanoi. That topped the 8.65% Bloomberg survey median of eight economists and followed a revised 8.81% in the second quarter, marking the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2022. The government is aiming for at least 10% growth this year as it moves up the value chain on a path to high-income status by 2045. The latest numbers suggest the plan is on track, with a heavy push on infrastructure adding heft to momentum.
The statistics office said most sectors posted gains, supported by government efforts to deliver double digit growth in 2026, while structural reforms are improving governance and how resources are used. Across January through September, the economy expanded 9.01%.

September's trade beat was eye-catching: exports jumped 39.1% from a year earlier versus a 26.6% estimate, and imports climbed 45.8% compared with expectations of 38.1%. After eight straight months of deficits, the trade balance flipped to a $1.27 billion surplus in September.
Inflation came in at 5.08% for September versus the same month a year ago, narrowly below the 5.10% projection. Transport and construction costs stayed elevated because of the Iran war. The government's goal is to hold inflation to 4.5% for the year.

President Donald Trump on Thursday said he is following the upcoming Brazilian election “very closely,” referring to Brazil as a “very important" country. "The people of Brazil are fantastic people,” he told reporters outside the White House. “It’s a very important election.”
The U.S. State Department later announced the suspension of its consular services in Brazil ahead of the election taking place on Sunday, citing unspecified security concerns. “U.S. citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other U.S. diplomatic facilities,” the security alert advised.
Recommended Stories
Brazilians are heading to the polls for a set of federal elections spanning congressional and gubernatorial races, alongside the first round of the presidential election votes. It’s set to be a decisive moment for Latin America’s largest nation, as the region has seen a shift toward the right in recent years. An Oct. 25 runoff is expected, as polls show a tight contest between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted last year for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election loss. Trump led the conservative voices denouncing the conviction, referring to the trial as a “witch hunt.”
While Trump has acknowledged his active interest as Brazil votes on its political future, there are concerns he could be too involved. Trump and his Administration have been accused of attempting to interfere with the high-stakes overseas election.
In a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in late September, Democratic lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over what they referred to as “the Administration’s coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election.”
“Over the course of President Trump’s second term, we have seen U.S. officials engage in a sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” the lawmakers said in the Sept. 24 letter, signed by 30 House Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who caucuses with the Democratic Party.
In another letter sent to Rubio on Monday, three Democratic Senators voiced similar concerns about potential U.S. interference.
“This effort first escalated sharply during the summer of 2025, with the [U.S.] Administration deploying tariffs and targeted sanctions to attempt to shape the Brazilian Supreme Court’s verdict in the trial of former President Jair Bolsonaro on charges of attempting to foment a military coup to stay in power,” said the Senators, noting that the tariff pressure escalated in July this year when the Trump Administration moved to impose a new 25% tariff on many imports from Brazil—a decision labeled a “lamentable milestone” by Lula’s office.
The Senators argued that the “campaign directed at Brazil’s authorities resumed with the appointment of Darren Beattie as a senior advisor on Brazil issues in the State Department.” Beattie served as a White House speech writer in Trump’s first term, but was axed for attending a gathering of white supremacists. He returned to the fold early on in Trump’s second term. When serving as undersecretary for public diplomacy and public affairs last year, he called one of Brazil’s Supreme Court Judges a “key architect of the censorship and persecution complex directed against Bolsonaro and his supporters.”
Accusing the Trump Administration of using “diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening [Brazil’s] democratic institutions [and] undermining confidence in Brazil's electoral process,” the Senators closed the letter by asking the Administration to “commit to recognizing the certified outcome of Brazil's 2026 democratic elections.”
The White House has staunchly rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s elections.
“Conservative leaders are winning elections across the Western Hemisphere on their own merit because everyone sees the success of President Trump’s policies,” said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly in a statement to TIME. “These claims are nonsense.”
President Lula has also expressed concern over Trump’s interest in his country’s election. “I have already told President Trump it is very important that the U.S. do not interfere in Brazil’s elections,” he said in a Sept. 22 interview. “Brazilian elections are the concern of the Brazilian people. American elections are the concern of the American people.”
Lula added that he is “very worried about Marco Rubio,” claiming that the U.S. Secretary of State “is very closely connected to Bolsonaro’s people,” though he stressed that this was only “suspicion.” TIME has reached out to the State Department for comment.
How the Trump Administration has been accused of meddling in Brazil’s affairs
Trump has not formally endorsed either candidate in Brazil’s presidential race, but his defense of former Brazilian President Bolsonaro, who was last year sentenced to 27 years in prison, is well documented.
After Trump criticized the trial proceedings as a “terrible thing” in July 2025, the Trump Administration increased pressure on Brazil’s government by imposing punishing 50% tariffs— extended in part due to Bolsonaro’s treatment in the courts—and directing the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate trade relations with the country.
The State Department added to the pressure later that same month, when Rubio called Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes’ actions a “political witch hunt against Jair Bolsonaro” and announced visa restrictions on Moraes, unspecified judicial allies, and their immediate families.
Feliciano de Sá Guimarães, an associate professor at the Institute of International Relations at the University of São Paulo, says Lula was able to turn the economic pressure into a political argument of his own.
“Lula realized that he could play [these threats] in his favor for electoral purposes,” he says, explaining that Lula used the concept of “rally round the flag,” meaning that once a country is targeted by another, “the incumbent President can rally the people and say, ‘look our sovereignty is under attack.’”
The theme of sovereignty has featured prominently in Lula’s 2026 government manifesto, which points to Trump’s tariffs as damaging the Brazilian economy.
Guimarães says the U.S. Administration has since slightly altered its strategy, favoring an approach that could instead benefit Lula’s opposition.
Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, Rubio, and Vice President J.D. Vance at the White House in May. Trump later described the Brazilian lawmaker as a “smart young man, who loves his country very much.” Shortly after that meeting, the U.S. Administration on May 28 designated Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho—two Brazilian gangs—as terrorist organizations, with Bolsonaro appearing to take credit for the move in the media.
Guimarães says the issue may have resonated in Brazil due to public concerns about crime.
“Brazilians are so desperate with the situation of crime in the country that they are resorting to support any initiative, whether it's coming from the federal government or a foreign power to fix the problem,” Guimarães explains, so the move could be seen to strengthen Bolsonaro’s chances with the electorate.
Economic pressure has continued as well. After ordering the USTR to investigate Brazil’s trade practices last year, the office imposed 25% tariffs on the country in July under Section 301, for what it described as unfair trade practices.
Other disputes have further heightened diplomatic tensions. At the end of July, Brazil denied visas to two U.S. State Department officials, accusing them of trying to interfere in the upcoming election. Shortly afterward, Brazilian Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti had her U.S. visa revoked.
Is the Trump Administration influencing Latin America’s rightward-turn?
Since returning to office, Trump has sought to exert U.S. influence more directly across Latin America.
In November 2025, the Trump Administration released its National Security Strategy, which highlighted a return to U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere and the beginning of the implementation of the "Donroe Doctrine," an informal term for Trump’s reinterpretation of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.
“The corollary of the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ is trying to stop the influence of extra regional powers in Latin America, mainly China,” says Guimarães.
Trump has also showcased his support for right-wing candidates across the region.
In response to Trump’s endorsement, House Democrats had sent a letter to Rubio expressing concern over what they said was “the brazen interference of senior U.S. officials, including President Trump” in Colombia’s election. “This interference involves the full-throated endorsement of Abelardo de la Espriella, a candidate with a profoundly troubling record that appears to run counter to U.S. interests and potentially to U.S. laws,” the lawmakers said.

Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, has since adopted a friendlier posture toward the U.S. Administration, enabling access to the country’s oil. The proposed partnership would involve the SCA through its affiliated Timsah Shipbuilding Company and would cover a range of maritime activities, including port development, marine construction, dredging, shipbuilding and training.
Rabie said the authority is seeking to expand beyond the Egyptian market and strengthen its presence in Africa by contributing to major development and infrastructure projects.
“The Suez Canal aspires to open new markets in the African hinterland and to participate seriously in development efforts,” Rabie said.
He added that the SCA is ready to transfer its technical and operational expertise to Kenya and contribute to the development of the country’s maritime infrastructure.

high_priority_articles.title: AGOA Lifeline to 2028 and a China Deal in Motion: Kenya's Two-Track Trade Strategy - Wansom AI
high_priority_articles.summary: AGOA Lifeline to 2028 and a China Deal in Motion: Kenya's Two-Track Trade Strategy  Wansom AI
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Summary
- AGOA extended to 31 December 2028: passed by the US Senate on 8 August, signed on 4 September 2026, and welcomed the same day by Trade CS Lee Kinyanjui.
- Same rules: existing eligibility, product coverage and the third-country fabric provision for apparel are retained.
- Retroactive refunds: general customs duties paid on qualifying entries during the lapse after 30 September 2025 can be reclaimed through US Customs, with processing within 90 days. Reciprocal tariffs, fees and interest are excluded.
- Kenya's stake: AGOA apparel exports were worth about Sh60.6 billion in 2024; apparel is about 70% of Kenya's exports to the US, and EPZ apparel firms employ more than 66,000 people.
- China Early Harvest: in force since May 2026, it gives duty-free access to about 98.2% of Chinese tariff lines, alongside China's zero-tariff offer to 53 African countries from 1 May.
- CADEPA next: Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi says Kenya is ready to begin comprehensive negotiations. A full agreement is not yet signed, and Kenya is expected to open its own market in return.
- Trade-law issues: the fragility of unilateral preferences, rules of origin and SPS barriers, EAC Common External Tariff constraints on bilateral concessions, and WTO rules for reciprocal agreements.
AGOA: A Two-Year Lifeline, Finally Signed
What AGOA is: The African Growth and Opportunity Act, enacted by the United States in 2000, grants duty-free access to the US market for more than 6,000 product lines from eligible sub-Saharan African countries. It is a unilateral preference: Washington grants it, sets the eligibility conditions, and can withdraw or let it lapse. Kenya gives nothing in return under AGOA itself.
A turbulent two years:
| Date | Development | 
|---|---|
| 30 September 2025 | AGOA authorisation lapses; Kenyan exports to the US face ordinary duties | 
| 3 February 2026 | President Trump signs a one-year extension to 31 December 2026, applied retroactively | 
| 8 August 2026 | US Senate passes an extension to 31 December 2028 | 
| 13 August 2026 | Trade CS Lee Kinyanjui welcomes the Senate vote | 
| 4 September 2026 | President Trump signs the extension into law; Kinyanjui welcomes it the same day | 
What the extension provides:
| Element | Detail | 
|---|---|
| Duration | Duty-free access for eligible exports to 31 December 2028 | 
| Framework | Existing AGOA framework, eligibility requirements and product coverage retained | 
| Apparel | The third-country fabric provision, which lets AGOA apparel use fabric from outside Africa, continues | 
| Retroactive relief | Refunds of eligible duties paid during the lapse after 30 September 2025, claimed through US Customs and Border Protection and to be processed within 90 days | 
| Scope of refunds | General ad valorem customs duties only, not interest, merchandise processing fees, anti-dumping or countervailing duties, or specialised reciprocal tariffs | 
Kenya's exposure. Apparel is the heart of Kenya's AGOA trade:
- Apparel is about 70% of Kenya's total exports to the US, and more than 70% of its textile and apparel exports go to the US.
- AGOA apparel exports were worth about Sh60.6 billion in 2024, according to Economic Survey figures cited by the Trade Ministry.
- The 43 Export Processing Zone apparel firms employ more than 66,000 Kenyans directly.
- Beyond apparel, AGOA supports duty-free entry for cut flowers, tea, coffee and macadamia nuts.
The limits of the lifeline. AGOA removes ordinary US customs duties on eligible goods. It does not by itself shield Kenyan goods from other US tariff measures, which is why the refund carve-outs matter. The extension also runs out at the end of 2028, so the question of a longer-term, reciprocal arrangement with the US remains open.
Kenya–China: From Early Harvest to a Full Agreement
The framework. CADEPA, the China–Africa Development Economic Partnership Agreement (also called the Agreement on Economic Partnership for Shared Development), is China's model for bilateral economic partnership agreements with African states. Negotiators describe a concluded CADEPA as equivalent to a full free trade agreement. Kenya is among the first African countries to formalise its first stage.
How it unfolded:
| Date | Development | 
|---|---|
| April 2025 | President Ruto's state visit to China; relations elevated to an "All-Weather Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" | 
| 15 January 2026 | Kenya announces conclusion of the Early Harvest Arrangement | 
| March 2026 | Early Harvest Agreement signed; President Ruto describes negotiations on a bilateral deal as finalised | 
| 1 May 2026 | China applies zero tariffs on all tariff lines to 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations; Kenya's Early Harvest takes effect, covering the same lines | 
| 30 September 2026 | Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi says Kenya is ready to begin comprehensive negotiations on all aspects of CADEPA | 
Reading the two statements together. The March remark is best read as referring to the Early Harvest Agreement, an interim, tariff-focused package. On 30 September, Mudavadi described the next stage: comprehensive negotiations covering everything else a full agreement would contain. The broader agreement has not yet been negotiated or signed.
What the Early Harvest gives Kenya. Duty-free access to China for about 98.2% of Chinese tariff lines. Coffee, tea, avocados, macadamia nuts, flowers and horticultural products are among the beneficiaries. According to China's ambassador, Guo Haiyan, avocado oil exports have risen about 700%, coffee exports have nearly doubled, and aquatic products, including sea cucumbers, are up about 350%.
What Kenya offers in return. Unlike AGOA, the arrangement is not one-way. Reports indicate that Kenya will also open its market further to Chinese goods. The scope of Kenya's concessions, and how they sit with its EAC Common External Tariff obligations, are central questions for the comprehensive talks.
The imbalance it aims to address. In 2024, Kenya imported about US$4.3 billion of goods from China, mostly machinery, electronics and vehicles, while exporting about US$197 million, mostly primary commodities. The government's stated aim is to raise export volumes and move Kenyan exports up the value chain.
The Trade-Law Analysis: Two Very Different Instruments
|  | AGOA (United States) | Early Harvest / CADEPA (China) | 
|---|---|---|
| Legal nature | Unilateral US statute granting preferences | Bilateral agreement, moving towards a reciprocal partnership agreement | 
| Who decides | US Congress and the President | Both governments, by negotiation | 
| Reciprocity | None required from Kenya | Kenya also expected to open its market | 
| Duration | Fixed: to 31 December 2028, unless renewed | Interim arrangement pending a comprehensive agreement | 
| Main risk | Lapse, or loss of eligibility after annual review | Scope of Kenya's concessions and their effect on local industry | 
1. The fragility of unilateral preferences
AGOA's value is high, but so is its uncertainty. Eligibility depends on criteria set by US law, including market-economy and rule-of-law conditions and a requirement not to undermine US national security or foreign policy interests, assessed in annual reviews. Congress can let the programme lapse, as it did in 2025, or attach new conditions. AGOA also does not shield Kenyan goods from other US tariff tools, which is why the refund provision excludes specialised reciprocal tariffs. Two years of predictability is valuable, but it is not a long-term guarantee.
2. Rules of origin decide who actually benefits
Preferences only help goods that qualify. For AGOA apparel, the third-country fabric provision is decisive: it lets Kenyan factories use imported fabric, often from Asia, and still qualify. Most non-apparel goods must meet AGOA's value-content rules. Under the China arrangement, Kenyan goods will need to meet China's origin and sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) requirements. For agricultural products, those include market-access protocols and registration with Chinese customs. Zero tariffs do not remove those conditions.
3. The EAC constraint on reciprocal deals
Kenya is part of the EAC Customs Union, with a Common External Tariff applied by all Partner States. That limits how far Kenya can unilaterally cut its own tariffs for Chinese goods. Concessions on the Kenyan side will need to be designed with the CET in mind, through mechanisms the EAC framework allows, or coordinated with Partner States. The same issue arose when Kenya pursued bilateral trade talks with the US. It will be a central legal question in comprehensive CADEPA negotiations.
4. WTO and preference erosion
Under WTO rules, a full reciprocal agreement between Kenya and China would generally need to cover substantially all trade to qualify as a free trade area under GATT Article XXIV, although arrangements among developing countries can also be notified under the more flexible Enabling Clause. Early Harvest arrangements are typically treated as interim steps towards that end. Meanwhile, China's zero-tariff offer to 53 African countries means Kenya's tariff advantage over other African exporters in China is limited. The distinctive value of a Kenyan CADEPA lies in legal certainty, binding commitments and the non-tariff provisions a comprehensive agreement could add.
5. AfCFTA and diversification
The two tracks sit alongside Kenya's African Continental Free Trade Area commitments. Better access to the US and China does not replace regional integration. Firms that build supply chains within Africa may gain under AfCFTA rules of origin while selling into both markets.
What It Means for Each Stakeholder
Apparel manufacturers and EPZ firms
The biggest winners of the AGOA extension. Two years of certainty lets factories accept multi-season orders from US brands, commit to new capacity and keep workforces in place. The third-country fabric provision continues, so current sourcing models

high_priority_articles.summary: Uzbekistan Proposes One-Stop Center for Migrant Workers Heading to Russia  The Times Of Central Asia
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan has proposed establishing a one-stop center where citizens planning to work in Russia could complete key migration procedures before departure.
The initiative was discussed at a meeting between Uzbekistan Migration Agency Director Muhsinxo‘ja Abdurahmonov and Russian Ambassador to Uzbekistan Alexey Yerkhov.
The Migration Agency also wants Russian-language examinations to be available in the regions so applicants do not have to travel to Tashkent. It said the necessary infrastructure has been prepared in four regions.
Uzbekistan is proposing that citizens travel to Russia for specific vacancies. Prospective workers would know their employer and working conditions in advance.
In 2025, Tashkent and Moscow considered conducting medical examinations and Russian-language tests at branches of Russian universities in Tashkent and Jizzakh.
The latest initiative comes as work-related travel from Uzbekistan to Russia has declined. In January-June 2026, Uzbek citizens made more than 1.1 million entries into Russia declaring work as the purpose of their trip, down 13.2% from a year earlier. Across Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan, work-related entries fell by about 15%, from more than 2.3 million to 1.9 million. The figures count border crossings rather than individual workers, meaning the same person can be counted more than once.
Despite fewer work-related entries into Russia, cross-border remittances to Uzbekistan reached $9.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up 13% year-on-year. The Central Bank attributed the increase to sustained demand for labor and relatively high wages in traditional destination countries for Uzbek migrant workers, as well as the strengthening of national currencies.
The Central Bank also pointed to signs of diversification in the geography of labor migration. Transfers from the United Kingdom increased by 62% year-on-year, those from European Union countries by 27%, and those from the United States by 19%.

high_priority_articles.title: Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
high_priority_articles.summary: Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Tajikistan announced that it is now receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran, opening a potential new energy source for a country whose fuel supplies have long been dominated by Russia.
The deliveries began in late August, Tajikistan's Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency, following talks between the two countries on expanding cooperation in the oil and gas sector.
The ministry has not disclosed the volume of the shipments, their commercial terms, or how the oil and petroleum products were transported to Tajikistan.
The move also raises questions about potential US secondary sanctions for doing business with Iran, particularly as Washington has stepped up pressure on Tehran's oil revenues.
A US Treasury official, who asked not to be identified, said the department would not comment on specific allegations of sanctions violations but warned that Iran's petroleum and petrochemical sectors are subject to increased sanctions risk.
"Anyone operating in that sector incurs that risk themselves should they continue to choose to do so," the official said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL.
Tajikistan has asked Iran to supply up to 2.55 million tons of crude oil and petroleum products annually, including gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. But that figure represents a requested or potential volume rather than the amount currently being delivered.
The potential shift toward Iranian supplies could give Dushanbe another option, although the economics and logistics of moving large quantities of Iranian oil to landlocked Tajikistan remain unclear.
The oil deal comes as Tajikistan faces continued uncertainty over fuel supplies from Russia, which accounted for more than 91 percent of the country's petroleum-product imports in the first half of 2026.
Russian fuel shortages and export restrictions, exacerbated by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, have prompted Tajikistan and other Central Asian countries to seek alternative sources.
In July, Tajik authorities said they were in talks with neighboring countries to secure future supplies.
Tajik political analyst Parviz Mullojonov said the search for Iranian supplies was being driven in part by Tajikistan's need to secure alternative energy sources.
Warming Relations
The Iranian deliveries also come amid a broader warming of relations between Dushanbe and Tehran.
"The report that Iran has started to sell oil to Tajikistan comes as the relation between Dushanbe and Tehran is warming and they're becoming closer," said Edward Lemon, president of the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs.
Tajikistan and Iran, which share close linguistic and historic ties, established diplomatic relations in 1992. Tajikistan's Foreign Ministry says bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the previous year, and that the countries have signed more than 200 agreements and memorandums.
At a meeting of the Tajik-Iranian intergovernmental commission in Dushanbe in May, officials discussed energy, transport, industry, investment, science, and technology.
The two countries also have defense ties. In 2022, Iran and Tajikistan inaugurated a drone-manufacturing facility in Dushanbe, designed to produce Iranian-designed Ababil-2 drones.
But relations between the two countries have not always been close. Ties deteriorated sharply in the mid-2010s, with Dushanbe wary of Tehran's alleged support for Tajikistan's banned Islamic Renaissance Party.
In 2017, Dushanbe also accused Tehran of involvement in a series of political killings in Tajikistan in the 1990s, allegations that Tehran denied.
The relationship began to thaw in the early 2020s. In 2022, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon visited Tehran, and the two sides pledged to strengthen diplomatic, trade, and security ties.
The Sanctions Question
A Tajik delegation that visited Tehran in August held talks with Iranian officials responsible for oil products and railways, with energy supplies and logistics among the issues discussed, according to the Tajik Embassy in Tehran.
But closer energy cooperation with Iran could also create complications for Dushanbe as Washington increases pressure on Tehran.
Under US Iran sanctions authorities, foreign companies and financial institutions can face sanctions for certain significant transactions involving Iranian petroleum and petroleum products.
The US Treasury official also emphasized the secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and said any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the US financial system.
The Treasury Department has repeatedly warned of sanctions exposure linked to Iranian oil and in August announced an expansion of conduct that could trigger secondary sanctions.
A State Department spokesperson said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL that the United States would continue to "disrupt, expose, and dismantle" Iranian military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyberoperations, and illicit oil trade that sustain what Washington calls the Iranian regime's "malign behavior."
The spokesperson called on the international community to join the United States in holding those involved accountable.
Lemon said the possibility of secondary sanctions should factor into Dushanbe's calculations as it expands purchases from Iran.
"Tajikistan could of course become one of those countries," he said.
At the same time, Lemon said, the scale of Tajik-Iranian cooperation could be important in determining how seriously Washington views the relationship.
"The scale of cooperation is quite low, much in contrast to countries such as Russia or China," he said.
Mullojonov said Tajikistan was seeking to balance relations with the United States, Russia, China, Turkey, and other powers while pursuing its own economic interests.
"Maintaining a diplomatic balance is incredibly difficult because these global powers often have conflicting agendas," Mullojonov said.
For now, it remains unclear whether Iranian oil can become a substantial alternative to Russian supplies.
RFE/RL contacted Tajikistan's Energy and Foreign Affairs ministries for comment but has not received a response.

high_priority_articles.title: Korea Alcohol Group Shifts From Ethanol to Semiconductor Materials Value Chain - thelec.net
high_priority_articles.summary: Korea Alcohol Group Shifts From Ethanol to Semiconductor Materials Value Chain  thelec.net
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Korea Alcohol Group is shifting its portfolio toward semiconductor materials, moving the focus from ethanol and commodity chemicals to higher-value semiconductor materials. The group has built a circular semiconductor materials value chain connecting its affiliates, covering the process from production and distribution to resource recycling. It is also establishing a production hub in Yesan, South Chungcheong Province, bringing together major materials affiliates.
According to industry sources on Oct. 1, Korea Alcohol Group has expanded its semiconductor materials business through affiliates including KC&A, Korea Alcohol Industrial, ENF Technology, UBM, PURIT and PAM Technology. The growing share of high-value semiconductor products has translated into improved earnings.
Korea Alcohol Industrial's standalone sales in the first half of this year rose 8.6% from a year earlier to 153.2 billion won. Operating profit increased 123% to 13.6 billion won. PURIT reported sales of 82.6 billion won and operating profit of 12.5 billion won, up 19.3% and 64.8%, respectively. ENF Technology reported consolidated sales of 349.9 billion won and operating profit of 52.2 billion won, increases of 8.7% and 16%, respectively.
Korea Alcohol Industrial is the only company in South Korea producing normal butyl acetate, according to the company. It began as an ethanol producer in 1984 and entered the electronic materials market in 1999 after completing an electronic-grade normal butyl acetate plant in Ulsan. Normal butyl acetate is an organic solvent used to control the dissolution performance and volatility of semiconductor thinners. Thinners are solvents used in semiconductor photolithography to dilute photoresist (PR) or remove residual PR from the edge of wafers. Korea Alcohol Industrial's official materials identify normal butyl acetate and electronic and semiconductor materials among its businesses.
PURIT, established in 2010 to recover and refine waste organic solvents, has expanded its portfolio into high-purity chemicals for semiconductors. It currently produces high-purity organic solvents used in semiconductor photolithography, including propylene glycol monomethyl ether (PGME), propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA), ethyl 3-ethoxypropionate (EEP) and ethyl lactate (EL).
Among these products, PGME and PGMEA are supplied as raw materials for semiconductor thinners and other products manufactured by ENF Technology. EEP is supplied to Dow Chemical and Dongjin Semichem, while EL is supplied to Dongjin Semichem and others. Semiconductor materials accounted for more than 80% of PURIT's sales in the first half of this year, at 66.8 billion won.
ENF Technology has also shifted its focus from displays to semiconductor materials. Semiconductor materials sales began surpassing display materials in 2020. They now account for about 65% of total semiconductor-related sales. The company supplies thinners, etchants, strippers, cleaning solutions, monomers and polymers used in semiconductor photolithography and etching processes. Semiconductor materials sales have recently increased, led by hydrofluoric acid (HF)-based etchants that the company has successfully localized. ENF Technology's official materials describe its portfolio as including process chemicals for semiconductor and display manufacturing.
The group has also expanded its product portfolio by adding affiliates. In 2021, ENF Technology acquired a stake in UBM to enter the chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) slurry market. CMP slurry is a material made by mixing abrasive particles and chemicals used for wafer planarization. Earlier this year, ENF Technology increased its stake in PAM Technology, a joint venture with Japan's Morita Chemical Industries, making it a consolidated subsidiary. PAM Technology produces hydrofluoric acid-based buffered oxide etchant (BOE) and ammonia water, a raw material. ENF Technology's official materials identify UBM as a semiconductor CMP slurry company and PAM Technology as a producer of HF/BOE etchants.
The group has established a structure linking the businesses of its affiliates from raw-material sourcing and distribution through basic chemical materials, advanced semiconductor materials, and recycling and resource circulation. KC&A sources chemical raw materials in South Korea and overseas, while Korea Alcohol Industrial and PURIT produce high-purity electronic-grade solvents. ENF Technology uses those materials to make semiconductor process products such as thinners. PURIT also operates a waste organic-solvent recycling business using waste generated during manufacturing processes. KC&A describes its role as supplying raw materials to affiliates including Korea Alcohol Industrial and ENF Technology.
The group is also building a large production hub bringing together its major materials affiliates. Korea Alcohol Industrial, ENF Technology and PURIT are establishing an integrated campus in the Yesan 2 General Industrial Complex in South Chungcheong Province, with a combined investment of 450 billion won. PURIT has moved fastest on construction. It plans to invest about 45 billion won and complete preparations for production in the first half of 2027. The investment could be increased to as much as 100 billion won depending on future demand. Korea Alcohol Industrial and ENF Technology have secured sites with investments of 14.3 billion won and 31.8 billion won, respectively.
The group plans to continue expanding each affiliate's business around semiconductor materials. Korea Alcohol Industrial has set a target of 805 billion won in consolidated sales, 88.2 billion won in operating profit and a return on equity (ROE) of at least 12% by 2030.

The USMCA entered into force on July 1, 2020, between the United States, Mexico, and Canada (collectively, the Parties).[1]
Article 34.7.1 of the USMCA provides that the Agreement must terminate 16 years after the date of entry into force—
i.e.,
July 1, 2036—unless each Party confirms that it wishes to continue the Agreement for a new 16-year term. Pursuant to Article 34.7.2 of the USMCA, the Free Trade Commission (Commission), composed of the three Parties, convened on July 1, 2026, to conduct the first joint review of the operation of the Agreement. At that meeting, the United States did not agree to extend the Agreement for a new 16-year term. As such, pursuant to Articles 34.7.4-6 of the USMCA, the Commission will meet to conduct a joint review annually until each of the three Parties confirms its wish to extend the term of this Agreement for another 16-year period or the term of the Agreement expires, whichever is earlier.
In accordance with Section 611 of the
United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement Implementation Act

high_priority_articles.title: Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games - UNITED24 Media
high_priority_articles.summary: Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games  UNITED24 MediaPutin observes military drills in the Urals involving troops from China and other nations  AP NewsRussia rehearses invasion and occupation of Central Asian country during military exercises  Українська правдаChinese PLA completes Russia’s Center-2026 exercise with 99A tanks, unmanned systems; expert highlights lessons from modern warfare  Global Ti...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Russia rehearsed an offensive into the territory of a neighboring Central Asian state and the creation of a “security zone” there during the Center-2026 military exercises, which involved more than 47,000 personnel across multiple training grounds and the Caspian Sea.
According to Interfax on October 2, Russian forces practiced repelling an attack in the South Ural direction before switching to offensive operations intended to retake captured territory and establish a security zone on neighboring land.
“The coalition grouping of forces is repelling the main attack in the South Ural direction, has restored the situation, and since October 2 has been conducting offensive operations to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone on adjacent territory,” Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov told Russian leader Vladimir Putin during the exercises.
Russian officials did not identify the neighboring state involved in the scenario. Kazakhstan, however, is the only Central Asian country that shares a land border with Russia. It directly borders Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where the main stage of Center-2026 was held, and also has access to the Caspian Sea, where another part of the exercises took place.
The drills ran from September 28 through October 3 and involved more than 47,000 military personnel across 11 training grounds and the Caspian Sea, according to Russian officials. Around 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft and helicopters, and 77 warships and support vessels were involved in the exercises.
At the Chebarkul training ground in the Chelyabinsk region, Russian forces deployed tanks, motorcycles, artillery, drones, aircraft, and other military equipment. A T-14 Armata tank was among the systems demonstrated during the exercises.
The Caspian Flotilla simultaneously conducted an anti-landing operation, while four Russian long-range aircraft practiced strikes against what the exercise scenario described as critical enemy infrastructure.
Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan also participated in Center-2026. Kazakhstan was represented during the exercises by an operational group.
Putin attended the drills at the Chebarkul training ground on October 2. Russian officials said units directly participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine were not deployed for the exercises, although the training incorporated battlefield experience gained during the invasion.
More than 2,000 Russian personnel who had fought in Ukraine participated in Center-2026, according to Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yevkurov, while equipment previously used on the battlefield was also incorporated into the drills.
The Center-2026 scenario therefore extended beyond defending Russian territory: after repelling the simulated attack, Russian-led forces were tasked with crossing into neighboring territory and establishing a security zone there.
Earlier, Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russia planned to train around 600 Chinese troops in 2025 using battlefield experience gained during its war against Ukraine. The program reportedly focused on tank warfare, artillery, air defense, and combat engineering, marking a broader expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Beijing.

high_priority_articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion - BBC
high_priority_articles.summary: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion  BBC‘At war’: Allies’ relationship implodes  News.com.auThe Turner Report: Yankee invaders (no, not the tourists)  Niagara NowCanada should hold on to military relationship with U.S., former defence chief says  theglobeandmail.comConrad Black: Carney's invasion musings  National Post
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.
Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.
Why it is unlikely to happen
A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
Not always the best of friends
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.
But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.
In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."
What a US invasion could look like
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.
He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.
He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.
Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.
But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.
